units.passage: The use of generative AI of any kind in these assignments poses a risk that such work, its purposes, and ultimately any academic benefit it could provide the student, may be undermined and will be graded accordingly.
units.why: 'will be graded accordingly' warns that AI use in voice-developing assignments is reflected in the grade, a consequence stated in advance but with no specific penalty; P37 is the nearest type, though it is vague, so I note the fit.
units.fit_note: No concrete penalty is stated, only that the work 'will be graded accordingly' because AI undermines its purpose.

units.passage: Using generative AI to complete any assignment or exam, or any portion thereof, without express permission from the instructor, will constitute an academic integrity violation and may result in penalties.
units.why: 'may result in penalties' states that penalties are possible but names none; the clause is a penalty warning, nearest P37, though no concrete penalties are given for AI specifically.
units.fit_note: Penalties are only mentioned, not specified; the general sanction list appears in 3710.6.

units.passage: Yale regards cheating as a serious oense, for which the standard penalty is two semesters of suspension.
units.why: "the standard penalty is two semesters of suspension" for cheating states a concrete penalty; it names cheating, not AI, and applies to AI misuse only through the AI note that calls it a breach of integrity: P37.
units.fit_note: About cheating generally; does not name AI.

units.passage: to construct works with ample citations that are not flagged when run through a plagiarism detector such as Turn It In.
units.policy: ChatGPT text with citations is not flagged when run through a plagiarism detector such as Turn It In.
units.why: Output "not flagged when run through a plagiarism detector such as Turn It In" says detectors miss AI text, so detectors are not dependable, P39 (fit is partial since it speaks of plagiarism checkers).
units.fit_note: Coder A: Concerns a plagiarism checker (Turnitin) failing to flag AI text rather than an AI detector being unreliable. | Coder B: Says a plagiarism detector misses ChatGPT text; it does not say not to use detectors.

units.passage: *Note that AI detectors have been found to be inaccurate for AI misuse. See the references below.
units.policy: AI detectors have been found to be inaccurate for AI misuse.
units.why: "AI detectors have been found to be inaccurate for AI misuse" tells instructors detectors are unreliable, P39.

units.passage: Instructors should exercise caution when using AI detection tools and prioritize their own professional judgment when evaluating student work.
units.why: "Instructors should exercise caution when using AI detection tools and prioritize their own professional judgment" says detectors are not to be relied on, so P39.

units.passage: While automated detection tools may seem like a convenient solution, it’s crucial to understand their limitations. For example, they cannot definitively identify AI-generated content and have been known to produce false positives, which can unfairly implicate students. Overreliance on these tools can lead to incorrect labeling of student work as AI-generated, potentially damaging trust and causing harm to innocent students.
units.why: Detectors 'cannot definitively identify AI-generated content and have been known to produce false positives' states the unreliability of detectors, the core of P39, informs.

units.passage: One word of caution: Students may be able to circumvent these tools.
units.why: 'Students may be able to circumvent these tools' warns that AI detectors can be fooled, a reliability limit on detectors: P39, informs.

units.passage: Insufficiency of GAI Detectors: AI detectors are principally problematic for the high numbers of false positives they currently return (as of February 2025).
units.policy: AI detectors are principally problematic for the high numbers of false positives they currently return (as of February 2025).
units.why: 'AI detectors are principally problematic for the high numbers of false positives' says detectors are unreliable, which is P39.

units.passage: As of February 2026, WSU has cancelled its contract with Turnitin for its AI Detection software.
units.why: "WSU has cancelled its contract with Turnitin for its AI Detection software" is an institutional decision not to use a detector, so P39.

units.passage: The cancellation of Turnitin’s AI detection software aligns WSU with other R1 institutions who have banned its use in academic integrity, including UC-Berkeley, Colorado State University, Indiana University, Michigan State University, Oregon State University, and the University of Washington.
units.why: "aligns WSU with other R1 institutions who have banned its use in academic integrity" gives a peer comparison as part of the rationale for cancelling AI detection, so it belongs with P39 (do not rely on AI detectors); a rationale is general and informs.
units.fit_note: Also benchmarks the cancellation against peer R1 institutions that banned AI detection.

units.passage: Although disputed, Turnitin claims that they have a false positive detection rate of 1-2% (i.e., false positive meaning a paper is written by a human but flagged as AI generated). Other studies placed this value higher, especially for students who are neurodivergent or have English as a second language.
units.why: The page cites a Turnitin "false positive detection rate of 1-2%" and higher rates in other studies, evidence that detectors are unreliable: P39.

units.passage: Every false positive has the potential to lead to the submission of a case of a violation of academic integrity against a student.
units.why: "Every false positive has the potential to lead to the submission of a case" gives a reason for dropping detection; reasons for not relying on detectors are P39.

units.passage: These cases negatively impact student trust and wellbeing.
units.why: False positives cause "growing distress and anger" among students and harm "student trust and wellbeing"; a rationale against detection, P39.

units.passage: Between 2023-2025, 33% of all Review Board cases related to allegations of inappropriate AI use led to a finding of not responsible because AI detection was submitted independent of any other supporting evidence.
units.why: "33% of all Review Board cases related to allegations of inappropriate AI use led to a finding of not responsible because AI detection was submitted independent of any other supporting evidence" is evidence from the university's own cases that detector-only cases fail (P39). Not P55, which is about learning. The university reports it, so admin; evidence, so over-time; informs.
units.fit_note: Evidence concerns detector reliability and case outcomes, not learning.

units.passage: The output from the Turnitin detector is instructor facing and is not student facing. This means students are not aware of potential issues with their work prior to the detector’s report to the instructor. Therefore, proactive communication from a student to their instructor about potential issues is not available.
units.why: "not student facing" means students cannot see detector flags before the instructor, a reason against the detector, so P39.

units.passage: Currently, WSU does not endorse the use of any AI detection tool for several reasons.
units.why: "WSU does not endorse the use of any AI detection tool" is a stance against detectors, P39.

units.passage: AI detection tools remain unreliable and academic misconduct remains an area of concern for faculty, especially those who strongly believe AI misuse has taken place but do not feel they have enough evidence to file with DOSO.
units.why: The report says "AI detection tools remain unreliable", a statement that detectors cannot be trusted (P39).

units.passage: AI detection tools also remain unreliable and are something that we should not consider using.
units.why: AI detection tools 'are something that we should not consider using', advice against detectors (P39). (Final codes after reconciliation: unit_stance neutral; see resolution_why.)

units.passage: Do not rely solely on the results of an AI detection tool when considering whether to speak with a student about a possible violation of the Honor Code.
units.why: 'Do not rely solely on the results of an AI detection tool' with 'can generate false positives' says detectors are unreliable and cannot be sole evidence; P39, instructor, when-misuse, should-not.

units.passage: Rigorous testing has shown that AI detectors are unreliable in most practical scenarios (Sadasivan, 2023).
units.why: "Rigorous testing has shown that AI detectors are unreliable in most practical scenarios" says detectors cannot be trusted as proof; this is P39 (do not rely on detectors) stated as a fact, so modality informs.

units.passage: AI detectors have also been shown to be biased against English language learners (Liang, 2023).
units.why: The page says 'AI detectors have also been shown to be biased against English language learners', a further reason not to rely on detectors, aimed at instructors choosing how to enforce. It is a fact (informs) about detectors, so P39 (do not rely on detectors) with an equity topic.
units.fit_note: Adds a specific bias against English language learners as a reason detectors are unreliable. The bias is in detectors, not in generative AI itself.

units.passage: Work flagged by AI detection tools is not definitely AI-generated.
units.why: States flagged work 'is not definitely AI-generated': detectors are unreliable (P39).

units.passage: Non-native English speakers and beginning writers might use simple sentence structures or phrasing and tone that differ from standard English. This can cause AI detection tools to mistake these as attempts of using AI writing tools.
units.why: Warns detectors may mistake non-native speakers' or beginners' phrasing for AI: detector unreliability (P39).
units.fit_note: Names a specific bias against non-native and novice writers.

units.passage: Compare the assignment of concern to a student’s previous work. Dramatic inconsistencies in voice, style, and grasp of concepts may indicate the use of AI-generative tools. You may even identify inconsistencies within a single submitted assignment.
units.why: "Compare the assignment of concern to a student's previous work" uses prior work as evidence of misuse; P40 is the nearest (process evidence) though it names no tool.
units.fit_note: Evidence is comparison with the student's earlier work, not software, commit history or logs. | Identification by comparing against the student's earlier work and noting inconsistencies in voice and style, not software or logs.

units.passage: Gently inquire about their writing process and sources. Students are often eager to discuss insights from their work and learning about their writing process (when they started the assignment, what was their drafting/editing process, what tools were used, etc.) may help determine if unauthorized resources were used.
units.why: "Gently inquire about their writing process and sources" is a conversational check to identify unauthorized use, so P40 (process evidence) is the nearest fit; P57 is about talking before escalating.
units.fit_note: Process evidence is gathered by asking the student, not from logs or software. | Asking the student about drafting and tools to detect misuse, not software or logs.

units.passage: Verify citations and quotes. AI tools often generate fictional sources and misattribute source material.
units.why: 'Verify citations and quotes. AI tools often generate fictional sources' tells instructors to check sources to spot AI use; P40 is nearest (methods to identify misuse).
units.fit_note: Detection by checking fabricated citations rather than by software or process records. | Checking cited sources for fabrication as an identification technique.

units.passage: As for detecting if students' typed academic work contains AI-generated text, the best way is to honestly grade that work and look for errors.
units.why: "the best way is to honestly grade that work and look for errors" uses output quality as the way to spot AI text, nearest P40.
units.fit_note: Detection by ordinary grading for factual errors, not by software or process records. | Detection by reading for errors, not software or logs.

units.passage: Another option is to use a 'similarity detector' (often mistakenly called a 'plagiarism detector') like Turnitin.
units.why: "Another option is to use a 'similarity detector'... like Turnitin" to flag text, so P40.

units.passage: The Turnitin plagiarism software package will continue to be available to WSU Faculty, Instructors, and Students via Canvas.
units.why: The page keeps Turnitin's plagiarism package: "will continue to be available ... via Canvas"; a similarity checker remains available, which is P40.
units.fit_note: Only the similarity (plagiarism) package remains; the AI detector is cancelled.

units.passage: Any submitted work may be reviewed for AI-generated content.
units.why: 'Any submitted work may be reviewed for AI-generated content' signals checking of submissions; P40.
units.fit_note: Says work may be reviewed for AI content, without naming a tool. Does not say how work is reviewed (software or reading).

units.passage: Note that we still have the Simcheck plagiarism detection tool which reports plagiarism flags to instructors who activate it in assignments in Canvas.
units.why: Says the Simcheck plagiarism tool reports flags to instructors who activate it in Canvas: a similarity check (P40).

units.passage: In the absence of an enterprise tool for AI detection, instructors may find other tools to be helpful in your investigation of student work, as long as they are used appropriately to protect student personal information.
units.why: Says instructors 'may find other tools to be helpful' if they protect student personal information: detectors allowed with a privacy condition (P40).
units.fit_note: Adds the condition of protecting student personal information.

units.passage: ATUS recommends beginning an evaluation using the plagiarism detection tool built into Canvas assignments.
units.why: ATUS recommends beginning with the plagiarism tool built into Canvas: similarity check first (P40).

units.passage: and may require work to be completed using specific applications, platforms, or LMS features that preserve evidence of the work process.
units.why: "may require work to be completed using specific applications, platforms, or LMS features that preserve evidence of the work process" uses process evidence to identify misuse, P40.

units.passage: This class abides by Yeshiva University’s academic integrity policy . All assignments will be analyzed by Turn-it-in for plagiarism and AI use.
units.why: "All assignments will be analyzed by Turn-it-in for plagiarism and AI use" in the general template uses detection software to find misuse (P40).

units.passage: When potential issues of academic integrity arise, it is helpful for students to show provenance of their work. Google Docs has a robust version history that can help and it is recommended that all written work be composed in Google Docs. All students have access to the Google suite of tools through their YU account.
units.why: "it is recommended that all written work be composed in Google Docs" uses version history as evidence of provenance (P40).

units.passage: All written assessments must be completed from start to finish in google docs. No written work should be done outside of google docs.
units.why: "All written assessments must be completed from start to finish in google docs" is a required platform for process evidence (P40).

units.passage: Use Turn-It-In. Turn-it-in has been required for written work at YC and SCW since 2019 as a plagiarism detection tool. Turn-it-in now also has a built-in AI scanner. It systematically underreports the AI likelihood but is a good automatic screen.
units.why: "Use Turn-It-In" with its "built-in AI scanner" tells instructors to run a similarity and AI scan (P40).

units.passage: Anything with a 5-10% AI likelihood in turn-it-in should be scrutinized further.
units.why: "Anything with a 5-10% AI likelihood in turn-it-in should be scrutinized further" uses a detector score as a screen with a threshold (P40).
units.fit_note: Gives a numeric threshold at which a detector score triggers closer review; also says the scanner underreports AI likelihood.

units.passage: Relying solely on ChatGPT for problem-solving may hinder the development of problem-solving skills that require personal analysis and critical thinking.
units.policy: Relying solely on ChatGPT for problem-solving may hinder the development of problem-solving skills that require personal analysis and critical thinking.
units.why: "Relying solely on ChatGPT for problem-solving may hinder the development of problem-solving skills" is a skill-building rationale, P41.

units.passage: Since the goal is for you to develop your critical thinking skills, ideas, and critical perspectives on the class materials,
units.why: The template gives a reason: "the goal is for you to develop your critical thinking skills", a skill-building rationale for the ban (P41).

units.passage: I also think this feature feeds into giving students the right answer too quickly.
units.why: 'Where is the progressive struggle of figuring things out?' criticizes giving the right answer too quickly; I chose P41 over P43 because it is about practice, not exposure on exams.

units.passage: Having taught some upper-level courses, I see that students need to struggle, with the struggle of learning mathematics.
units.why: The chair argues 'students need to struggle, with the struggle of learning mathematics', an argument that shortcuts undermine skill-building (P41).

units.passage: But these same tools can also pose a threat to our mission when they interfere with student learning or when they are used to violate our policies on academic integrity and/or data privacy
units.why: "pose a threat to our mission when they interfere with student learning" gives a learning-based reason for caution; it also mentions integrity and privacy, but the learning concern leads, so P41.
units.fit_note: Also names academic-integrity and data-privacy violations as threats, not only lost skill-building.

units.passage: But these same tools can also pose a threat to our mission when they interfere with student learning or when they are used to violate our policies on academic integrity and/or data privacy.
units.why: 'these same tools can also pose a threat to our mission when they interfere with student learning or when they are used to violate our policies' gives the risk rationale; nearest P41 (AI shortcuts the practice that builds skill), but it also names integrity and privacy, so fit_note.
units.fit_note: A: Also names integrity and data-privacy violations as threats, which P41 does not capture. B: Also names academic-integrity and data-privacy violations as threats, not only lost skill-building.

units.passage: Artificial Intelligence tools are increasingly accessible and powerful—but using them in FYE is counterproductive and defeats the core principles of growing as a learner.
units.why: FYE 'Do NOT Use': 'using them in FYE is counterproductive and defeats the core principles of growing as a learner'; AI shortcuts learning, P41.

units.passage: While AI can assist in many areas, true learning happens when you engage directly with the material, think critically, and express your own ideas.
units.why: 'true learning happens when you engage directly with the material, think critically, and express your own ideas'; P41.

units.passage: The most rewarding experiences will come from grappling with ideas and communicating them in your own voice.
units.why: "The most rewarding experiences will come from grappling with ideas and communicating them in your own voice" explains the no-AI choice by learning, P41.

units.passage: We want you to do the independent reading, critical thinking, analysis, and writing that will best contribute to your development over the course of your degree program.
units.why: 'We want you to do the independent reading, critical thinking, analysis, and writing' explains wanting students to build skills themselves; P41.

units.passage: We believe there is significant long-term value in your developing these capacities unmediated by AI tools.
units.why: "Significant long-term value in your developing these capacities unmediated by AI tools" explains limits by learning value, P41.

units.passage: Some generative AI tools undermine student learning and prevent instructors from evaluating a student’s knowledge of a subject or ability to communicate.
units.why: "Some generative AI tools undermine student learning and prevent instructors from evaluating a student's knowledge" gives the reason AI is limited: outsourcing undermines learning and assessment (P41).
units.fit_note: Also says AI prevents instructors from evaluating knowledge.

units.passage: And, although there are many tools (technological and human) that exist to support your ability to be efficient in this application, to be effective in your use of existing tools, you need to be skilled in your own right.
units.why: "to be effective in your use of existing tools, you need to be skilled in your own right" gives the reason that foundational skills are the aim of the class, P41 (AI shortcuts the practice that builds skill).
units.fit_note: Also says work should demonstrate critical thinking and the student's own ideas.

units.passage: The use of generative AI of any kind in these assignments poses a risk that such work, its purposes, and ultimately any academic benefit it could provide the student, may be undermined and will be graded accordingly.
units.why: Gives the reason assignments develop 'the student's voice and perspective' and AI 'may be undermined': AI shortcuts the practice that builds the skill (P41), not a fairness or career argument.
units.fit_note: Rationale is tied to reflective, research and interpretive assignments, not to coding practice. Also says affected work "will be graded accordingly", an unspecified grading consequence (coded separately).

units.passage: But if students rely on AI assistance before building their own skills, the result can be a loss of the struggle that deepens learning.
units.why: "if students rely on AI assistance before building their own skills, the result can be a loss of the struggle that deepens learning" gives skill-building as the reason to limit AI: P41.

units.passage: AI can strengthen those capacities or hollow them out, depending on how you use it.
units.why: "AI can strengthen those capacities or hollow them out, depending on how you use it" explains that AI use can undermine the capacities students come to build, so it is P41 (AI shortcuts practice that builds skill).

units.passage: Sometimes that means restricting it now so that you become a stronger thinker, and a better user of AI, later.
units.why: "Sometimes that means restricting it now so that you become a stronger thinker, and a better user of AI, later" justifies restriction as sequencing toward later skill, matching P08 (permission staged as skills develop) in spirit; I chose P41 since no staging mechanism is given.
units.fit_note: Frames a restriction now as a way to become a better AI user later; P41 does not capture the later-use angle.

units.passage: Work that AI does for you is potentially learning you did not do.
units.why: "Work that AI does for you is potentially learning you did not do" gives the skill-building reason for restricting AI (P41).

units.passage: AI should augment learning and skill development, never substitute for it or undermine it.
units.why: "AI should augment learning and skill development, never substitute for it or undermine it" states the learning-centered principle (P41).

units.passage: and to restrict AI where its use diminishes the value of the human work.
units.why: "restrict AI where its use diminishes the value of the human work" lets instructors restrict AI where it diminishes learning (P41).

units.passage: Reduced Learning Engagement : Overreliance on AI may hinder deep engagement and cause a lack of understanding of course materials, leading to incomplete learning experiences.
units.why: "Overreliance on AI may hinder deep engagement and cause a lack of understanding of course materials" explains that AI can undermine learning (P41).
units.fit_note: Frames overreliance as reduced engagement rather than shortcutting practice.

units.passage: Some students may lack the foundational knowledge to understand why or how AI-generated content is inaccurate.
units.why: 'Some students may lack the foundational knowledge to understand why or how AI-generated content is inaccurate' says novices cannot judge AI output: P42, informs.

units.passage: The usefulness of these tools depends on the user’s understanding of the tool and subject matter knowledge of the material created.
units.why: "The usefulness of these tools depends on the user's understanding of the tool and subject matter knowledge" says value depends on user knowledge; nearest is P42 (novices cannot judge output).
units.fit_note: States that usefulness depends on user understanding and subject knowledge, without singling out novices or fundamentals.

units.passage: In some courses, it will make sense to restrict use of AI while students develop skills and become oriented to a field.
units.why: "In some courses, it will make sense to restrict use of AI while students develop skills and become oriented to a field" says restricting AI suits skill-building in some courses; P42 (fundamentals come first). P08 is not chosen because the text gives no later stage when AI is allowed. Modality may because it presents restriction as an option instructors may take, unit_stance restrict.
units.fit_note: Says restriction suits the skill-building period but does not say when it lifts. Framed as an option for some courses, not specific to novices or intro courses.

units.passage: Some students may lack the foundational knowledge to understand why or how AI-generated content is inaccurate. This presents an excellent teaching opportunity for you to demonstrate for your students generative AI's strengths and weaknesses.
units.why: Students lacking foundational knowledge may not see why AI content is wrong, an "excellent teaching opportunity" to "demonstrate... strengths and weaknesses"; so P44 (courses demonstrate AI use).
units.fit_note: Framed as teaching AI's limits to novices, not as a career skill.

units.passage: Identify the skills and approaches necessary to use GAI successfully in relevant fields, disciplines, or professions.
units.policy: Programs identify the skills and approaches necessary to use GAI successfully in relevant fields, disciplines, or professions, and how fields and professions use GAI that students should learn about.
units.why: Asks what skills students need 'to use GAI successfully in relevant fields, disciplines, or professions', treating AI use as a professional skill (P44).

units.passage: There may be a need to integrate AI literacy into certain curricula given employer demands and/or industry trends.
units.why: The report says AI literacy may need to be integrated into curricula "given employer demands and/or industry trends", a career reason to teach AI (P44).

units.passage: the restrictions you impose may hinder the development of skills and behaviors needed to engage thoughtfully in an AI-integrated world.
units.why: The page warns that 'the restrictions you impose may hinder the development of skills and behaviors needed to engage thoughtfully in an AI-integrated world'. It is a reason, addressed to instructors who are deciding what to impose, so it is rationale (informs) under P44 (effective AI use as a skill).
units.fit_note: Framed as a cost of banning AI, not as a statement that courses should teach AI use.

units.passage: The approach to AI use in this course and the inclusion of this acknowledgement in our work will help us to develop our skills for using AI while maintaining our academic integrity.
units.why: The sample says the approach "will help us to develop our skills for using AI while maintaining our academic integrity"; a reason that learning to use AI is a skill alongside integrity, P44.

units.passage: But students should also learn how knowledge is made and shared in their disciplines and in settings beyond the university, and how these methods may change in light of AI.
units.why: "students should also learn how knowledge is made and shared in their disciplines ... and how these methods may change in light of AI" gives a rationale that students learn AI-shaped professional methods, P44.
units.fit_note: Framed as learning how disciplinary methods change, not as employer expectations.

units.passage: we understand that students must be prepared to lead in an AI-infused world.
units.why: "students must be prepared to lead in an AI-infused world" gives preparation for AI-rich work as a reason to engage with AI: P44.

units.passage: Yale has the opportunity to serve as a model by adapting its curricula to prepare students to lead in advancing and considering the implications of AI.
units.why: "Yale has the opportunity to serve as a model by adapting its curricula to prepare students to lead" is an aspiration to prepare students for AI-rich work: P44.

units.passage: Protect academic integrity while helping students build the AI skills their future careers will require.
units.why: The bullet says to help students "build the AI skills their future careers will require", a career-readiness reason (P44).

units.passage: Develop responsible AI fluency appropriate to each discipline: the ability to use AI productively, evaluate and verify its output, recognize its limits, protect sensitive information, and take responsibility for work produced with its assistance.
units.why: The bullet aims at "responsible AI fluency": using AI productively, verifying output, taking responsibility; teaching effective AI use as a skill (P44).

units.passage: At the same time, AI is an important technology, and learning to use it well is part of preparing for your career.
units.why: "learning to use it well is part of preparing for your career" is a professional-skill reason to teach AI use (P44).

units.passage: Where AI use is appropriate, instructors are encouraged to place it in authentic disciplinary and professional contexts, so that students learn to use and evaluate AI in settings resembling those they will encounter beyond the classroom.
units.why: "instructors are encouraged to place it in authentic disciplinary and professional contexts" encourages teaching AI in professional settings (P44).

units.passage: Students can view AI tools, such as ChatGPT, Google Bard or Cluade 2, as collaborators to enhance academic endeavors.
units.policy: Students can view AI tools, such as ChatGPT, Google Bard or Claude 2, as collaborators to enhance academic endeavors.
units.why: "view AI tools ... as collaborators" frames AI as a collaborator; P45 is the nearest type though no existing integrity rules are mentioned.
units.fit_note: Calls AI a collaborator without tying it to collaboration or citation rules.

units.passage: Unauthorized Collaboration : AI tools might be used for improper collaboration, blurring individual contributions, and violating academic integrity.
units.why: "AI tools might be used for improper collaboration, blurring individual contributions, and violating academic integrity" treats AI as a collaborator under integrity rules (P45).
units.fit_note: Describes AI-enabled improper collaboration as an integrity violation rather than stating a classification rule.

units.passage: Instructors may use AI tools to assist with drafting feedback and analysis, but final academic judgments (grades, degree progress decisions, and disciplinary determinations) must always be made and confirmed by a qualified human.
units.why: "final academic judgments (grades, degree progress decisions, and disciplinary determinations) must always be made and confirmed by a qualified human" keeps humans deciding grades; P46 is nearest and the passage also covers progress and discipline.
units.fit_note: Also covers degree progress and disciplinary determinations, not only grades (P73). | Also covers degree-progress and disciplinary determinations (P73), not only grades.

units.passage: Grades and substantive evaluative judgments must be reviewed and confirmed by the instructor of record, consistent with Section 5.4.
units.why: "Grades and substantive evaluative judgments must be reviewed and confirmed by the instructor of record" keeps humans assigning grades (P46).

units.passage: If you plan to use AI detection software on student work, students should be explicitly informed of this.
units.why: "students should be explicitly informed of this" requires telling students when detection software will be used on their work; nearest P47 (instructor discloses own AI/tool use to students).
units.fit_note: Disclosure is about using a detection tool, not generative AI for grading or feedback. | Disclosure is about using a detector on student work, not instructor use of generative AI.

units.passage: What are the expectations for disclosure of GAI usage in these contexts?
units.why: Asks about 'expectations for disclosure of GAI usage' in faculty work, the instructor-disclosure type (P47).
units.fit_note: Question about disclosure expectations; recipient of disclosure is not specified. | A question about disclosure expectations for faculty use, not a commitment to disclose to students

units.passage: Transparent in how they are using AI to support the work of teaching. Do faculty indicate where AI was used to generate questions, assist with grading and feedback, or influence teaching decisions?
units.why: Faculty should indicate "where AI was used to generate questions, assist with grading and feedback, or influence teaching decisions", disclosure of instructor AI use (P47).

units.passage: When instructors thoughtfully acknowledge how AI has supported their work—in course design, writing, or research— they help students develop a more mature understanding of academic tools, agency, and intellectual ownership.
units.why: "When instructors thoughtfully acknowledge how AI has supported their work ... they help students develop a more mature understanding" asks instructors to disclose their own AI use: P47.
units.fit_note: Also frames the disclosure as modelling for students (P112). Presented as a way to teach students about academic tools and ownership, not as an obligation to disclose in grading.

units.passage: Faculty are expected to disclose substantial AI generation in course materials and feedback to their students.
units.why: "Faculty are expected to disclose substantial AI generation in course materials and feedback to their students" is instructor disclosure (P47).

units.passage: Lack of Transparency/Disclosure : Instructors should inform students whenever they use AI tools. Clear disclosure of the technology’s involvement in classroom activities helps maintain trust and avoid confusion.
units.why: "Instructors should inform students whenever they use AI tools" lists lack of transparency as unethical and asks instructors to disclose (P47).

units.passage: *Note: This page was written by ChatGPT (GTP-3.5) after providing information about responsible use of artificial intelligence for university students and making the most of such tools while maintaining academic integrity. It was edited from its original version by Alysia Ropp.

units.passage: In a private discussion with another faculty or TA in the meeting, the instructor can discuss concerns with the student, explain questionable areas of submitted work, and listen openly to students' processes and reasoning.
units.policy: In a private discussion with another faculty or TA present, the instructor discusses concerns with the student, explains questionable areas of submitted work, and listens openly to the student's processes and reasoning.
units.why: "listen openly to students' processes and reasoning" with "another faculty or TA in the meeting" is talking to the student and gathering context before escalating, P57.

units.passage: Consult with other professors or TAs for their opinion on whether the assignment submission appears suspicious. They may have insight into the student's typical writing style and capabilities.
units.policy: Instructors consult with other professors or TAs for their opinion on whether the assignment submission appears suspicious; they may have insight into the student's typical writing style and capabilities.
units.why: "Consult with other professors or TAs for their opinion" and "insight into the student's typical writing style" gather context from colleagues before escalating; nearest P57 (context before escalating), though P57 is about talking with the student.
units.fit_note: Coder A: The consultation is with colleagues, before or alongside speaking to the student. | Coder B: Gathering colleague opinion, not talking with the student; the use of typical writing style as evidence is not covered.

units.passage: Speak with the student privately to discuss the concerns. Don't accuse but explain the specific areas that seem unusual and ask the student to explain their process and reasoning. Listen openly.
units.policy: Instructors speak with the student privately, do not accuse, explain the specific areas that seem unusual, and ask the student to explain their process and reasoning.
units.why: "Don't accuse but explain the specific areas that seem unusual and ask the student to explain their process" is talking with the student first, P57.

units.passage: When concerns arise, consider having a conversation with the student about their work before making conclusions. This is not required, but can provide valuable context and may reveal legitimate explanations eliminating the need to file a report with OAI.
units.why: 'consider having a conversation with the student about their work before making conclusions' is the talk-before-escalating rule, P57; 'This is not required' makes it should.

units.passage: Please remember to provide the student an opportunity to respond to your concerns prior to reporting them to the Center for Community Standards.
units.why: Instructors should "provide the student an opportunity to respond to your concerns prior to reporting them"; talking to the student first before escalating, P57 (P64 is the hearing right).
units.fit_note: Also gives the student a chance to respond to concerns.

units.passage: Additionally, the Center for Community Standards requires that an attempt to meet with the student to discuss the concerns be made prior to submitting an academic integrity report.
units.why: CCS "requires that an attempt to meet with the student to discuss the concerns be made prior to submitting an academic integrity report"; talking before escalating, P57.
